title: SC: Child remains legitimate even if father is unnamed in birth certificate
summary: The Supreme Court (SC) has ruled that a child born during a valid marriage remains legitimate even if the father is not identified in the child"s birth certificate.

blocks.text: The Supreme Court (SC) has ruled that a child born during a valid marriage remains legitimate even if the father is not identified in the child’s birth certificate.

In a nine-page resolution, the SC Third Division granted a woman’s petition to correct her birth certificate to reflect her proper middle name and surname, as well as the date of her parents’ marriage.

“Under Article 164 of the Family Code, ‘children conceived or born during the marriage are legitimate.’ This means that legitimacy as a status attaches once a person is born within wedlock,” the Court said.

The petitioner’s parents were legally married when she was born. However, her mother registered her birth under her maiden surname, used her own middle name for her daughter and left the father’s identity blank because the couple were not on good terms at the time.
The High Court said Article 167 of the Family Code provides that a child remains legitimate even if the mother declares otherwise, including in the child’s birth certificate.
The petitioner grew up using her father’s surname in her school and employment records, including her Professional Regulation Commission identification card.
She discovered the discrepancies in her birth certificate only in 2017, prompting her to seek its correction.

The SC said substantial corrections to civil registry records may be sought under Rule 108 of the Rules of Court through adversarial proceedings, in which interested parties are notified and given the opportunity to contest the requested changes.
In her concurring opinion, Associate Justice Maria Filomena Singh also cited Rule 108, saying it may be used to correct entries in civil records that affect a person's legitimacy or filiation.

“A petition under Rule 108 is a procedural device to cancel or correct entries in the civil register, including entries relating to birth and filiation, subject to due process requirements,” Singh wrote.

She cited Section 2 of Rule 108, which allows the cancellation or correction of civil registry entries on valid grounds, including births, marriages, deaths, legitimations, adoptions, acknowledgments of natural children, judicial determinations of filiation and changes of name.

The Court ordered the concerned local civil registrar to amend the petitioner's birth certificate by replacing her middle name with her mother's maiden surname, changing her last name to her father's surname and indicating the date of her parents' marriage.
The resolution was penned by Associate Justice Japar Dimaampao and promulgated on April 7, 2026.— MCG, GMA News
